paragraphs: This list is used only for self-questioning and does not constitute hiring criteria, capability scores or an evaluation of position competence. This page corresponds to US O*NET/SOC 51-9071.06 Gem and Diamond Workers (the fixed Chinese index name is Gem and Diamond Workers; the industry often calls them diamond cutters, diamond graders, diamond sorters, diamond polishers, diamond setters, faceters, gem carvers, gemologists and gem cutters). The official scope is: fabricate, finish, or evaluate the quality of gems and diamonds used in jewelry or industrial tools. The core work includes assigning polish and symmetry and clarity grades to stones according to an established grading system; recording the clarity characteristics of stones with diagrams; examining the surface and internal structure of stones with optical instruments such as polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes to distinguish species, identify rare specimens or find flaws that affect value; locating and marking drilling or cutting positions on the stone being worked; securing stones with fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks; selecting grinding wheels for the task and mixing and applying abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents; polishing facets with the stone on a polishing machine holder; holding the stone against rotating laps and wheels and saws for cutting and shaping and grinding and polishing; measuring stone drilling and facet dimensions with precision measuring instruments to ensure they meet specification; grading rough diamonds by shape and size and color and quality; cleaving stones along pre-marked lines to remove flaws; determining specific gravity and key properties with prescribed chemical solutions; estimating the wholesale and retail value of stones based on price guides and market fluctuations; replacing and truing and sharpening blades and drills and laps; disassembling grinding and drilling and cutting and polishing and shaping equipment for cleaning and lubrication; adjusting the rotational speed of drilling mechanisms; and advising customers on stone selection and buying and selling diamonds and diamond jewelry for customers. The work is characterized by a controlled indoor environment, long periods of sitting, extremely high demands for precision and accuracy, and considerable dealings with external customers. The O*NET 2024 industry background is for the parent occupational group 51-9071: retail 34%, manufacturing 17%; gem and diamond workers are not separately listed, and the remaining 49% cannot be assigned to any specific industry on that basis.

90-minute paper exercise | Use the entry-section synthetic sample G1: 0.60 grams, angle 42.6° (specification 42.0°±0.5°), hole diameter 1.02 mm (specification 1.00±0.05 mm). Using the task statement's 1 carat = 0.20 grams and the assumed wholesale and retail prices of 100/130 yuan per carat, recompute the weight, tolerance and quote; draw the given P and L characteristics, and list the information gaps and hold points for review. Do not touch real stones, equipment or chemicals, and do not determine grade, scrap or issue a certificate based on the exercise.

Fit signals | The US O*NET 51-9071.06 work context shows: importance of precision or high accuracy 98% extremely important; indoors environmentally controlled 91% daily; email 88% daily, telephone 87% daily, face-to-face discussions 73% daily; continuous contact with others 74%; dealing with external customers or the public 71% extremely important; sitting 78% continuously or almost continuously; work schedule 88% regular; time pressure 68% once a week or more but not daily; exposure to hazardous conditions 99% and outdoors in all weather 97% and noise 82% all never; using hands to handle, control or feel objects and tools 19% and repetitive motions 24% both about half the time; the pace being determined by equipment speed 85% not at all important. If you can check details one by one under magnification for long periods, have patience for fine manual work, can record the basis for grading and measurement and value judgments clearly, and maintain professional boundaries when communicating with customers, this occupation's daily demands are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (51-9071.06): importance of precision or high accuracy 98% extremely important, sitting 78% continuously or almost continuously, responsibility for the health and safety of others 13% no responsibility, level of competition 15% extremely competitive, typical workweek less than 40 hours 12%; the work is mainly indoor, solitary, focused fine processing and grading, and dealing with external customers is 71% extremely important, meaning conclusions and quotes will be questioned directly by customers. This occupation takes unworked gems and diamonds as its object, and one facet angle or symmetry deviation, one clarity or color grading misjudgment, one measurement or value estimate error, or one misjudgment of cutting or cleaving direction can cause irreversible material loss and trigger value and liability disputes; grading and valuation conclusions also involve third-party certificates and transaction settlement. If you find it hard to maintain the stability and checking patience of fine work for long periods, or tend to give unsupported conclusions under customer pressure, treat these as real costs that need serious weighing.

Taking on judgment | True fit comes from whether you can do three things at once on the same gemstone task: do the processing and grading solidly (assign polish and symmetry and clarity grades per the grading system, record clarity characteristics with diagrams, examine surface and internal structure with optical instruments, cut and shape and grind and polish after securing and positioning, and measure dimensions with precision instruments), keep verifiability under control (leave a trail for the measurement and grading and valuation basis, use and record samples and tools and chemicals per procedure, and note errors and disagreements truthfully), and bear a definable position responsibility (be responsible for your own grading and measurement and processing results and your own records, and escalate matters involving certificate issuance and final value determination and transaction settlement per institutional procedure or hand them to a third party). It is suggested to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a grading record and clarity diagram, a securing and cutting and polishing plan, or a measurement and value estimate and assumption list for a fictional stone), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | This page's Gem and Diamond Workers corresponds to US SOC 51-9071.06, and the work can be divided into several categories: grading and quality evaluation — assign polish and symmetry and clarity grades to stones per the established grading system, record clarity characteristics with diagrams, and examine the surface and internal structure of stones with optical instruments such as polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes to distinguish species, identify rare specimens or find flaws that affect value; cutting and lapidary processing — locate and mark drilling or cutting positions on the stone being worked, secure the stone with fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks, select grinding wheels and mix and apply abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents, polish facets and hold the stone against rotating laps and wheels and saws for cutting and shaping and grinding; measurement and value assessment — measure stone drilling and facet dimensions with precision measuring instruments to ensure they meet specification, grade rough diamonds by shape and size and color and quality, cleave stones along pre-marked lines to remove flaws, determine specific gravity and key properties with prescribed chemical solutions, and estimate wholesale and retail value from price guides and market fluctuations; equipment maintenance and customer collaboration — replace and true and sharpen blades and drills and laps, disassemble grinding and drilling and cutting and polishing and shaping equipment for cleaning and lubrication, adjust the rotational speed of drilling mechanisms, and advise customers on stone selection and buy and sell diamonds and diamond jewelry. The four categories cycle in sequence: inspection and grading — securing and positioning — cutting and lapidary work and polishing — measurement and valuation — recording and review — escalation of anomalies and disagreements. This page does not conflate this occupation with the adjacent jewelry and precious metal workers or hand grinders and polishers or grinding machine workers or etchers and engravers or dental laboratory technicians.

O*NET and BLS occupational profile highlights | This page corresponds to US SOC 51-9071.06 Gem and Diamond Workers (a position under the production major group), with the official scope: fabricate, finish, or evaluate the quality of gems and diamonds used in jewelry or industrial tools. The core tasks listed by O*NET include: assign polish and symmetry and clarity grades to stones according to an established grading system (importance 85); record the clarity characteristics of stones with diagrams (85); estimate the wholesale and retail value of stones from factors such as price guides and market fluctuations (85); inspect stones during processing with a magnifying glass and jeweler's loupe and shadowgraph to ensure cutting angles and drilling positions are accurate (83); inspect diamonds or stones to determine shape and cut and width or select the cut that yields the largest and best quality stone (80); examine the surface and internal structure of stones with optical instruments such as polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes to distinguish species and identify rare specimens or find flaws (80); advise customers and others on stone selection to make attractive jewelry (77); locate and mark drilling or cutting positions on stones or molds with diamond bort and powered hand tools (70); secure stones with fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks in preparation for cutting and polishing and grinding and drilling and shaping (69); select shaping grinding wheels for the task and mix and apply abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents (65). Additional supplemental tasks include measuring stone drilling and facet dimensions with precision measuring instruments to ensure they meet specification (85), grading rough diamonds by shape and size and color and quality (79), polishing facets with felt or canvas polishing laps and polishing agents (77), holding stones against rotating laps and wheels and saws for cutting and shaping and grinding and polishing (75), replacing and truing and sharpening blades and drills and laps (64), securing stones to metal mountings with solder (61), immersing stones in prescribed chemical solutions to determine specific gravity and key properties (61), grinding drill points to specification and advancing the drilling point (53), cleaving stones along pre-marked lines with blades and jeweler's hammers to remove flaws (52), disassembling grinding and drilling and cutting and polishing and shaping equipment for cleaning and lubrication (47), and adjusting the rotational and reciprocating speed of drilling mechanisms (41). The most important work activities are updating and applying relevant knowledge (87) and identifying objects and actions and events (85), followed by getting information (80) and making decisions and solving problems (79) and thinking creatively (78) and estimating the quantifiable characteristics of products and events or information (77) and inspecting equipment and structures or materials (75) and judging the quality of objects and services (73) and processing information (73) and organizing and planning and prioritizing work (71).

Grading and processing note | Start with inspection and grading: first check the species and polish and symmetry and clarity of the stone per the established grading system and record the characteristics and diagrams, then per specification and authority determine the securing and positioning and cutting or drilling positions and the grinding wheels and abrasives and polishing agents, and after processing measure the drilling and facet dimensions with precision instruments and compare them with the specification; matters involving value estimation, certificate issuance, cleaving and splitting direction, chemical use or risk of material loss are reviewed and escalated per institutional procedure, and when grading or measurement disagreements or irreversible deviations occur they are handed to a senior grader or process supervisor.

BLS employment and wage basis | This page corresponds to US O*NET/SOC 51-9071.06 (Gem and Diamond Workers). The wages shown by O*NET under this occupation entry are on the parent occupational group 51-9071 Jewelers and Precious Stone and Metal Workers basis: 2025 median hourly wage 25.26 USD and median annual wage 52,540 USD; 10th percentile annual wage 35,580 USD, 25th percentile annual wage 39,520 USD, 75th percentile annual wage 69,810 USD, 90th percentile annual wage 87,540 USD (BLS OEWS 2025, presented via the O*NET national wage page). The above is the US national basis and the parent occupational group basis, is not separately listed precisely for this occupation, excludes employer benefit costs and overtime premium, and does not apply to other jurisdictions.

Safety and data boundaries | This page covers three types of requirements: first, work safety and health — gem processing involves high-speed rotating laps and wheels and saws and drills, dust and noise and chemicals and high-temperature soldering and sharp tools, so protective equipment and ventilation must be used per institutional procedure and work must stay within authorized limits, and matters involving chemicals and soldering must be handled per chemical and fire safety requirements; second, materials and customer assets — stones and diamonds awaiting processing are of high value and must be handed over and stored and recorded per institutional procedure, and chipping or damage or loss must be reported immediately; third, data and records — grading diagrams, measurement readings, valuation bases and customer and transaction information must be true and complete and kept per institutional requirements, and personal information and commercial information are managed on a minimum-necessary and authority basis. This page provides general notes only and does not constitute safety or legal or compliance or appraisal advice.

Records and collaboration | Record per institutional procedure the inspection and grading conclusions and clarity diagrams, the securing and positioning and cutting and grinding and polishing parameters, the measurement readings and specification comparison results, the valuation bases and assumptions, and equipment maintenance and anomalies and handling and handover matters; when grading or measurement disagreements, facet or symmetry deviations, material chipping or damage, or chemical or equipment anomalies are found, report immediately per authority and handle per procedure, and do not modify conclusions on one's own or backfill records after the fact.

Boundary conclusion | This page corresponds to US SOC 51-9071.06, and the core difference from adjacent positions lies in the object and the output: this occupation takes unworked gems and diamonds as its object, and its output is verifiable grading and clarity diagrams and measurement readings and processed facets and dimensions and the valuation basis; jewelers and precious stone and metal workers (51-9071 series, jewelry making direction) take precious metals and jewelry structures and settings as their object, and their output is finished jewelry and repair pieces; hand grinders and polishers (51-9023.00) take the hand grinding and polishing of general workpieces as their object and do not take on gem grading and value assessment; grinding machine workers (51-4033.00) take the operation of grinding and lapping and polishing equipment for metal and plastic workpieces as their object; etchers and engravers (51-9194.00) take the etching and engraving of surfaces such as metal and glass as their object; dental laboratory technicians (51-9081.00) take the making and adjustment of dental restorations as their object. The objects and outputs all differ, and grading conclusions and value determinations and processing parameters cannot be carried over across positions.

Core concept of adjacent positions | Most positions in the group and adjacent positions aim to get materials right and complete per standards at a fine-processing site and to be responsible for quality and value and responsibility; the difference lies in the object and the output: some take the grading and cutting of gems and diamonds as the object, some take precious metals and finished jewelry, some take the hand grinding and polishing of general workpieces, some take the operation of grinding equipment, some take surface etching and engraving, and some take dental restorations.

Core purpose of this occupation | With unworked gems and diamonds as its object, within the bounds of the grading system and specification and institutional procedures, convert rough or semi-finished stones into gems or diamonds with a clear quality grade and dimensions and a value basis: inspection and grading, securing and positioning, cutting and shaping and grinding and polishing facets, measurement and comparison with the specification, value estimation per price guides, recording and review, and review and escalation when deviations or disagreements occur, so that the grading and processing process and results are traceable.

Main objects and basis of adjacent positions | Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers rely on precious metal materials and jewelry structures and setting techniques and style requirements; hand grinders and polishers rely on workpiece surface requirements and hand grinding and polishing tools; grinding machine workers rely on grinding and lapping and polishing equipment and tolerance requirements for metal and plastic workpieces; etchers and engravers rely on etching and engraving patterns and depth requirements for surfaces such as metal and glass; dental laboratory technicians rely on dental restoration design orders and materials and precision requirements.

Main objects and basis of this occupation | The objects are unworked gems and diamonds and semi-finished faceted stones, the grading system (polish and symmetry and clarity and color and cut), diagrams and magnifying glasses and jeweler's loupes and polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes, fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks, grinding wheels and abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents, rotating laps and wheels and saws and drills, precision measuring instruments, prescribed chemical solutions, and price guides and market information, based on institutional process procedures and grading standards and specification and authority, and material safety and chemical safety and data and record requirements.

Gem and Diamond Workers (US 51-9071.06) processes or evaluates the quality of gems and diamonds used in jewelry and industrial tools, delivering grading records, clarity diagrams, facet dimensions and the valuation basis. Core process of adjacent positions | Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers focus on precious metal forming and soldering and setting and surface finishing; hand grinders and polishers focus on grinding and polishing workpiece surfaces with hand tools; grinding machine workers focus on operating grinding and lapping and polishing equipment to process metal and plastic workpieces; etchers and engravers focus on producing etched or engraved patterns on surfaces such as metal and glass; dental laboratory technicians focus on making and adjusting dental restorations per design orders.

Core process of this occupation | Inspect and grade per the grading system and record clarity diagrams, secure and position per specification and determine the cut or drilling plan, cut and shape and grind and polish facets, measure drilling and facet dimensions with precision instruments and compare with the specification, estimate value per price guides and market factors, record and review the grading and measurement and valuation basis, and review and escalate when deviations or disagreements occur; every step must leave a trail per institutional procedure and authority and be reviewable by a senior grader or process supervisor.

Main outputs of adjacent positions | Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers produce finished jewelry and repair pieces and craft records; hand grinders and polishers produce hand-ground and polished pieces meeting surface requirements and records; grinding machine workers produce ground and lapped and polished workpieces meeting tolerances and equipment operation records; etchers and engravers produce parts with etched or engraved patterns and craft records; dental laboratory technicians produce dental restorations and making and adjustment records.

Main outputs of this occupation | Verifiable grading conclusions and clarity diagrams and measurement readings (polish and symmetry and clarity grades, drilling and facet dimensions), processed faceted stones and shaping and polishing results, rough diamond grading results by shape and size and color and quality, determination records for specific gravity and key properties, wholesale and retail value estimates and assumptions formed from price guides and market factors, and equipment maintenance and anomaly and handling and handover records.

Responsible parties for adjacent positions | Responsibility for positions in the group and adjacent positions is usually defined by the institution and process procedures and quality standards and authority, and the objects of responsibility are mostly the institution and customers and product quality and delivery deadlines.

Responsible party for this occupation | This occupation is responsible for its own grading and measurement and processing conclusions and its own records, and for securing and positioning and cutting and grinding and polishing and measurement completed per procedure; matters involving certificate issuance and final value determination, the buying and selling and settlement of gems or diamonds, decisions on cleaving and splitting direction, chemical use and equipment repair and material loss handling are decided by a senior grader or process supervisor or a designated institutional position with the corresponding authority, and this occupation does not replace their decisions.

Authority and approval of adjacent positions | The authority of positions in the group and adjacent positions comes from institutional authorization and process procedures and quality standards and usually does not include authority to decide final value determination and transaction settlement and customer disputes on their own; matters involving quality disputes and customer claims and process changes should be handed to a supervisor or quality and business position.

Authority and approval of this occupation | Inspection and grading and securing and positioning and cutting and grinding and polishing and measurement must be carried out within institutional authorization and process procedures and specification; matters involving certificate issuance and final value determination and settlement, decisions on cleaving and splitting direction, chemical use and equipment repair, and customer dispute and claim handling should be escalated or handed over per the rules to a senior grader or process supervisor or a designated institutional position, and conclusions must not be issued beyond authority or high-value materials handled without authorization.

Conclusion boundaries of adjacent positions | Conclusions for positions in the group and adjacent positions are mostly limited to the process and the workpiece and the individual's duties, and usually do not constitute a final determination of finished product quality or transaction value or customer disputes; conclusions across processes and institutions and standard systems have limits to their applicability.

Conclusion boundaries of this occupation | Personal conclusions state only verifiable grading and clarity diagrams and measurement facts and distinguish measured values from reading errors and estimated values; no unauthorized judgment may be made about certificate issuance or final transaction value or whether a material can continue to be processed; matters involving grading or measurement disagreements, material chipping or damage, chemical or equipment anomalies, and valuation and settlement disputes must be escalated or handed over, and the basis must also withstand review by senior graders and process supervisors and third-party testing and regulatory inspection.

Pre-employment check notes | The following six items are used to check item by item before applying and starting, so as not to infer actual duties and authority from a job title or promotional language; the check results should be based on written recruitment information, the labor contract, the job description and the institution's process and grading procedures, and should be continuously confirmed after starting. This page lists only check directions and does not constitute a formal conditions list for any institution. Special note: this occupation involves high-value materials and irreversible processing, so be sure to confirm the position's actual object (diamond grading, gem cutting, jewelry setting, testing laboratory, industrial diamond products) and the equipment and chemicals and authority boundaries.

Check point notes | Positions with similar names differ greatly in duties: some focus on diamond and gem grading and diagram records, some on cutting and lapidary work and polishing, some on setting and jewelry making, some on testing and certification, and some on industrial diamond and abrasive products; different institutions also have different authority requirements for grading conclusions and value determination and equipment and chemicals and records and customer information management.

01 Actual duties and authority boundaries | Check whether the role really carries grading and measurement and processing, or is mainly sales assistance or counter appraisal or material organization; check the issuance and review authority for grading conclusions and clarity diagrams and value estimates, the decision path for cutting or drilling or cleaving direction, the handling and reporting path for material loss and damage, and the approval and record responsibility for processing parameters and process changes.

Check point notes | Gem processing involves high-speed rotating laps and wheels and saws and drills, dust and noise and chemicals and soldering heat and sharp tools, and involves the custody and handover of high-value materials, and usually requires dedicated safety and equipment operation and chemical training and material custody rules.

02 Safety and equipment and chemical and material custody requirements | Check whether the institution provides and enforces equipment protection and personal protective equipment (goggles and dust protection and ventilation and noise protection), chemical safety and ventilation and firefighting and emergency handling training, operating qualifications and authority for high-speed rotating equipment and soldering work, material custody and handover and logging and two-person verification requirements, and the reporting and escalation path and record retention and access rights for material chipping or damage or loss and equipment anomalies.

Check point notes | US O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone Three (medium preparation), usually requiring vocational training or an associate degree or related on-the-job experience, and registered apprenticeship opportunities exist such as Brilliandeer-Lopper and Gem Cutter (jewelry); jewelry and gem specialty schools and certificate programs (such as gemology and grading courses) can provide entry training. This description does not replace employer requirements for safety and process and equipment training.

03 Education and training and qualification requirements | Check whether high school or equivalent and a basic foundation in geometry and dimension and weight conversion are required, whether institutional training in grading and diagrams and optical instruments and cutting and lapidary work and polishing and equipment maintenance is provided, whether gemology and jewelry specialty courses or certificates (such as gemologist and diamond grading certificates) are required or preferred, and the institution's internal job assessment and retraining cycle and the conditions for obtaining certificate issuance authority.

Pay check suggestions | Check in writing the base wage, commission, piece rate, production bonus, various allowances, overtime premium and working hours arrangements; which apply depends on the actual contract. This page has no national evidence that these components are generally present among gem and diamond workers.

04 Wage, hours and contract basis | Check the composition of the offered pay (base wage, performance or piece rate, bonus, skill or certificate allowance, overtime or compensatory rest), the working hours and shifts and peak-season arrangements, the probation and assessment basis, whether pay is calculated by grading or number of processed pieces, and whether responsibility agreements and compensation and insurance clauses cover material loss and damage.

Check point notes | Interfaces with sales and customer service, testing and certification, purchasing and inventory, and process and equipment maintenance determine the responsibility boundaries for grading conclusions and valuation bases and material custody and processing delivery, and must be clarified in advance.

05 Interface authority with sales and testing and purchasing and process positions | Check the authority to communicate grading conclusions and valuation bases and customer explanations with sales or customer service positions, the path for confirming re-testing and issuing certificates and handling disputes with testing or certification positions, the way gems and diamonds and consumables are handed over and logged with purchasing and inventory positions, the equipment repair and parameter change path with process and equipment maintenance positions, and the role arrangement for crew shift handover and collaboration.

Check point notes | The traceability and trail requirements for grading diagrams and measurement readings and valuation bases and equipment maintenance and anomaly handling records determine the definition of quality and value and customer dispute responsibility, and the rules for version, modification, archiving, access and retention period must be clarified in advance (customer and transaction information must also be managed per personal information and commercial information requirements).

06 Records and data and trail requirements | Check the version, modification, archiving, retention period and access rights rules for inspection and grading conclusions and clarity diagram records, securing and positioning and cutting and grinding and polishing parameter records, measurement readings and specification comparison result records, valuation basis and assumption records, equipment maintenance and replacement and anomaly and handling records, and material custody and handover records and customer and transaction information; the burden of proof and cooperation obligations in quality and value disputes and regulatory inspections and customer communications; and the requirements that grading and measurement data be truthful and not modified after the fact.

The objects and outputs all differ, and grade determination and value determination and processing parameters cannot be carried over across positions.

Evidence note | The comparison objects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and publicly available sales material, and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and choice fit, and do not constitute qualification, hiring, price or value conclusions. The wages and employment of each occupation must be checked separately per their own SOC basis; this table makes no numerical comparison and does not use one occupation's wage as a proxy for another; this occupation's grading and valuation and certificate conclusions must also be confirmed per institutional standards and third-party testing requirements.

Preface | The following comparison is laid out in four columns: career direction — core work and outputs — key differences — which choice suits better. Gem grading and cutting, jewelry metalwork and setting, hand grinding and polishing of general workpieces, grinding equipment operation, surface etching and engraving, and dental restoration making often connect within the same fine-processing industry chain, but connection does not mean they are interchangeable; when choosing across directions you should re-learn material properties, processing principles, quality standards and equipment and chemical safety procedures and authority scope.

Key differences: this occupation takes unworked gems and diamonds as its object, completes grading and clarity records and measurement and cutting and lapidary work and polishing and value estimation, and is responsible for grade and material loss; the other positions center respectively on precious metal jewelry, general workpiece surfaces, metal and plastic grinding, metal and glass surface etching and engraving, and dental restorations, and usually are not responsible for the grading and value conclusions of gems and diamonds.

Better suited to people who are willing to check details one by one under magnification for long periods, have patience for fine manual work, can turn feel and observation into compliance with standards, and can accept the responsibility pressure of irreversible processing of high-value materials.

Core work and outputs: assign polish and symmetry and clarity grades to stones per the established grading system, record clarity characteristics with diagrams, examine the surface and internal structure with polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes, locate and mark drilling or cutting positions on the stone, secure the stone with fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks, select grinding wheels and mix and apply abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents, polish facets and hold the stone against rotating laps and wheels and saws for cutting and shaping and grinding, measure drilling and facet dimensions with precision instruments, grade rough diamonds by shape and size and color and quality, and estimate wholesale and retail value from price guides and market factors; the outputs are grading conclusions and clarity diagrams and measurement readings and processed faceted stones and the valuation basis (US SOC 51-9071.06).
This occupation: Gem and Diamond Workers (51-9071.06)

Key differences: jewelers and precious stone and metal workers take precious metal materials and jewelry structures and setting and surface finishing as their object, and their output is wearable finished jewelry and repair pieces; this occupation takes the grade and dimensions and value of the gems and diamonds themselves as its object, and its output is grading and measurement and processing conclusions, and usually does not take full responsibility for jewelry structure and setting forming, but the grading and dimensions of set stones must be consistent with this occupation's conclusions.

Better suited to people willing to take responsibility for precious metal forming and soldering and setting and finished jewelry delivery; this occupation leans more toward the grading and cutting and appraisal of gems and diamonds.

Core work and outputs: saw, file, solder, form, set, grind and polish precious metals per style and process requirements, assemble gem settings and fittings, repair worn and broken jewelry, and record materials and process and weight and fineness; the outputs are finished jewelry and repair pieces and process and material records.

Key differences: hand grinders and polishers take the hand grinding and polishing of general workpieces (such as metal parts and molds and woodworking and stone pieces) as their object, using hand tools and abrasives to meet surface requirements; this occupation takes gems and diamonds as its object, requires determining grade and cut per the grading system and controlling facet angles and dimensions per specification, and involves irreversible material value judgments.

Better suited to people willing to take on hand surface treatment of various workpieces and deliver per feel and surface requirements; this occupation leans more toward gem grade determination and precise dimension control.

Core work and outputs: grind, lap, polish, deburr and finish workpiece surfaces with hand tools and abrasives and polishing wheels, check surface roughness and appearance and record; the outputs are hand-worked pieces meeting surface requirements and operation records.
Grinding and Polishing Workers, Hand (51-9023.00)

Key differences: grinding machine workers mainly operate grinding and lapping and polishing equipment to process metal and plastic workpieces, with dimensional tolerance and surface quality and equipment parameters as the output; this occupation takes gems and diamonds as its object, and grading and value judgment and optical inspection are its irreplaceable parts, with vastly different material properties and degrees of irreversibility.

Better suited to people willing to take responsibility for grinding equipment setup and parameter adjustment and tolerance control; this occupation leans more toward grading and valuation and gem material processing.

Core work and outputs: install and adjust grinding wheels and fixtures and tooling, set grinding and lapping and polishing parameters, process metal and plastic workpieces and measure dimensions and surface quality, replace and true grinding wheels and check equipment status; the outputs are ground and lapped and polished workpieces meeting tolerances and equipment operation records.

Key differences: etchers and engravers produce patterns and text on surfaces such as metal and glass, emphasizing pattern and depth and appearance consistency; this occupation centers on light transmission and internal structure and grade evaluation, emphasizing internal characteristics and optical properties and value grades.

Better suited to people willing to take responsibility for surface pattern and depth control and appearance inspection; this occupation leans more toward determining and processing the internal and optical characteristics of gems.

Core work and outputs: coat resist layers and expose and etch surfaces such as metal and glass per the drawing or engrave patterns and text with hand engraving tools, control depth and edge quality and check appearance, and maintain etching solutions and equipment; the outputs are parts with etched or engraved patterns and text and craft records.
Etchers and Engravers (51-9194.00)

Key differences: dental laboratory technicians produce dental restorations with design orders and materials and oral fit precision, subject to medical and hygiene regulation and the design order; this occupation produces gem and diamond grade and value and dimensions and usually does not involve medical regulation and human fit, but both are fine handcraft and dimension-control-intensive work.

Better suited to people willing to make dental restorations per medical design orders and hygiene requirements; this occupation leans more toward the grading and cutting and appraisal of gems and diamonds.

Core work and outputs: select materials and colors per the design order, make and adjust restorations such as crowns and bridges and dentures and orthodontic appliances, control dimensions and occlusion and shape, check quality and deliver and record; the outputs are dental restorations meeting design requirements and making records.
Dental Laboratory Technicians (51-9081.00)

Occupational definition | This page's Gem and Diamond Workers corresponds to US SOC 51-9071.06 Gem and Diamond Workers, with the official scope: fabricate, finish, or evaluate the quality of gems and diamonds used in jewelry or industrial tools. The core tasks include: assign polish and symmetry and clarity grades to stones according to an established grading system; record clarity characteristics with diagrams; estimate wholesale and retail value from price guides and market fluctuations; inspect stones during processing to ensure cutting angles and drilling positions are accurate; inspect diamonds or stones to determine shape and cut and width; examine the surface and internal structure with optical instruments such as polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes to distinguish species, identify rare specimens or find flaws; advise customers on stone selection; locate and mark drilling or cutting positions with diamond bort and powered hand tools; secure stones with fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks; select grinding wheels and mix and apply abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents; measure drilling and facet dimensions with precision measuring instruments; grade rough diamonds by shape and size and color and quality; polish facets and hold stones against rotating laps and wheels and saws for cutting and shaping and grinding; replace and true and sharpen blades and drills and laps; immerse stones in prescribed chemical solutions to determine specific gravity and key properties; cleave stones along pre-marked lines to remove flaws; disassemble equipment for cleaning and lubrication; and adjust the rotational speed of drilling mechanisms. The outputs are grading conclusions and clarity diagrams and measurement readings and processed faceted stones and the valuation basis; the above is the US basis, and the positions and statistical basis in mainland China are explained separately on this page.

This occupation's O*NET interest code is RC (Realistic—Conventional), corresponding to a willingness to carry out fine observation and manual processing and checking of physical objects under magnification (realistic) and to record and organize grading and measurement data per standards and procedures (conventional); this is consistent with the occupation's focus on gem grading and cutting and measurement and record handling and its extremely high precision requirement (98% extremely important). The questionnaire is only used to raise questions, not to judge suitability or whether you can start.

Boundary | The assessments and direction comparisons on this page are only used for self-questioning and exploration and do not constitute hiring criteria, capability scores, qualification judgments or evaluations of a position; entry is subject to institutional recruitment conditions, education and experience and training and assessment and authority. In particular, this occupation involves irreversible processing of high-value materials and rotating equipment and chemicals, so be sure to confirm the institution's equipment and chemical safety training and material custody and grading issuance authority requirements.

Direct answer | Tools and assessments cannot predict whether you will pass institutional training and assessment, whether you can stably complete grading and measurement and processing and records under magnification for long periods, and cannot replace real on-site practice. The most reliable way to judge is to use one real or simulated gemstone task to test how you inspect and grade and secure and process and measure and record, and whether you are clear about your own and the institution's authority and safety boundaries.

Gem and Diamond Workers | Produces verifiable grading conclusions and clarity diagrams and measurement readings and processed faceted stones and the valuation basis: assigns polish and symmetry and clarity grades per the grading system, records clarity characteristics with diagrams, examines surface and internal structure with optical instruments, cuts and shapes and grinds and polishes after securing and positioning, measures dimensions with precision instruments, and estimates value from price guides (US SOC 51-9071.06)
Can independently complete inspection and grading and clarity records and securing and processing and measurement and valuation per standards and specification and review

If it is hard to hold a sitting posture and stay focused for long periods, or irreversible processing of high-value materials and customer questioning are hard to bear, or you do not accept strict grade and dimension review, this occupation is not recommended.

Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers | Take precious metals and jewelry structures and settings as their object and produce wearable finished jewelry and repair pieces: saw, solder, form, set, grind and polish precious metals per style and process, assemble settings and fittings and repair wear and breakage
Has the ability to form and set precious metals and deliver finished jewelry
If you want to focus on the grading and cutting and appraisal of the gems and diamonds themselves rather than jewelry structure and setting forming, this direction is not recommended.

Hand grinders and polishers | Produce the hand grinding and polishing of general workpieces: grind, lap, polish, deburr and finish workpiece surfaces with hand tools and abrasives and polishing wheels, and check surface roughness and appearance and record
Has the ability to hand-treat and deliver the surfaces of various workpieces
If you want to focus on grade determination and precise dimension control rather than general workpiece surface treatment, this direction is not recommended.

Grinding machine workers | Produce the operation of grinding and lapping and polishing equipment for metal and plastic workpieces: install and adjust grinding wheels and fixtures and tooling, set processing parameters and measure dimensions and surface quality, replace and true grinding wheels and check equipment status
Has the ability to set up grinding equipment and adjust parameters and control tolerances
If you want to focus on grading and valuation and gem material processing rather than metal and plastic equipment processing, this direction is not recommended.

Etchers and engravers | Produce etching and engraving on surfaces such as metal and glass: coat resist layers and expose and etch per the drawing or engrave patterns and text with hand engraving tools, control depth and edge quality and maintain etching solutions and equipment
Has the ability to control surface patterns and depth and inspect appearance
If you want to focus on light transmission and internal structure and grade evaluation rather than surface pattern and text processing, this direction is not recommended.

Dental laboratory technicians | Produce dental restorations: select materials and colors per the design order, make and adjust crowns and bridges and dentures and orthodontic appliances, control dimensions and occlusion and shape and check quality and deliver
Has the ability to make and adjust restorations per medical design orders
If you want to focus on the grading and cutting and appraisal of gems and diamonds rather than medical restoration making, this direction is not recommended.

What kind of personality is better suited to gem and diamond workers? This occupation values more the ability to maintain stable observation and determination under magnification for long periods, sensitivity to internal characteristics and cut details and dimensional deviations, the stability of fine manual operations, and the rigor and traceability awareness to record the grading and measurement and valuation basis clearly, rather than a particular personality type; the interest code given by O*NET is RC (Realistic—Conventional), and the work styles emphasize caution and integrity and attention to detail and dependability, which can serve as a starting point for exploration.

Are introverts suited? Introversion and extroversion themselves cannot determine fit. O*NET shows 74% of respondents answered that continuous contact with others is required, and 71% consider external customer contact extremely important; you can test yourself with simulated handover and dispute communication, and do not mistake indoor focus for mostly solitary work.

The degree of extroversion itself cannot determine whether one can do well. This occupation has customer contact and fine operation and record requirements; the editorial suggestion is to use simulated handover and paper practice with G1 to observe communication, conversion and review separately, and not to infer competence from introversion or extroversion.
This round obtained no validity for MBTI type and competence in this occupation, so no best-fit type can be given; real training and authority are verified separately.

In Holland interests, which type is better suited to this occupation? The interest code given by O*NET is RC: realistic (fine observation and manual processing and checking of physical objects) and conventional (recording and organizing data per standards and procedures); it can be used to explore task preferences, not to predict performance.

This page obtained no specialized validity for these online personality and interest assessment scores on the performance of gem and diamond workers, and cannot make individual predictions from them. The O*NET interest code is an occupational-level description; behavioral evidence can be accumulated through task experience and institutional assessment.

The tasks involve geometry, angles, dimensions, weight and specific gravity conversion; you can first use G1 to check whether you can read specifications, convert units and review calculations. Specific mathematics training is checked against course and position requirements, and this page has no capability threshold or importance comparison study.

Does this occupation require high emotional intelligence? It requires emotional stability and the ability to cope with pressure, but does not require a particular assessment score. The work requires staying calm and acting per standards under long periods of focus and customer questioning or grading disagreements; long magnification work consumes attention and requires self-paced management.

Can the Enneagram be used to judge whether I suit it? No. The Enneagram is a self-exploration tool and does not constitute a conclusion about occupational ability or fit; judging fit should look at whether one can accurately complete grading and measurement and processing and records under magnification for long periods.

The editorial suggestion is to use approved simulated tasks to observe diagrams, measurement conversion and basis checking; it is unverified that a deliverable predicts fit better than a questionnaire, and real processing requires separately verified safety training and authority.

Fit signals: willing to grade and check per the system under magnification for long periods, able to keep fine manual work stable and record truthfully item by item, and to implement accuracy and review and material custody requirements at every step.

Caution signals: hard to hold a sitting posture and stay focused for long periods, or clearly uncomfortable with the irreversible processing of high-value materials and customer questioning, or unwilling to review and escalate per process when deviations and disagreements occur.

Verification suggestion: first use one simulated or real gemstone task to test inspection and grading and securing and processing and measurement and valuation and records, and understand the target institution's and position's requirements for training and assessment and equipment and chemical safety and material custody and grading issuance authority, before deciding whether to invest long term.

paragraphs: Boundary | This page lists the failure types and control points more commonly seen in this occupation in grading and cutting and measurement and valuation, to help identify and manage risk, and does not constitute safety or process or legal or quality or appraisal advice or a conclusion on any individual case; anything involving certificate issuance and final value determination, material chipping or damage handling, decisions on cleaving and splitting direction, equipment repair and chemical use, and the protection of customer and transaction information should be handled by a senior grader or process supervisor or a designated institutional position with the corresponding authority per organizational process and local regulations. What is described here is the general situation for fine processing and grading positions, and the specifics are subject to institutional process procedures and grading standards and quality systems and equipment and chemical safety requirements.

Editorial risk summary | Focus on failure of material and process, grading and measurement, records and handover, and information authority; the six cards are not an incidence or severity ranking, and real equipment, chemicals and handling follow procedures, training and authority.

Evidence scope | This page is based on the O*NET 51-9071.06 tasks and work context (importance of precision or high accuracy 98% extremely important, sitting 78% continuously or almost continuously, continuous contact with others 74%, dealing with external customers or the public 71% extremely important, exposure to hazardous conditions 99% and outdoors in all weather 97% and noise 82% all never, work schedule 88% regular, level of competition 15% extremely competitive) and work activities (updating and applying relevant knowledge 87, identifying objects and actions and events 85); work safety related to equipment and chemicals and soldering and dust and noise takes institutional safety procedures and the corresponding competent authority requirements as reference; the wage and employment figures serve as background information only and are not used for risk assessment.
The individual and the process supervisor; the institution and customer assets

Misjudging the cutting or drilling or cleaving direction, or improper securing and positioning, causing chipping or fracture; irreversible loss of high-value material, delivery delays and financial and reputational consequences

Before processing, check the cut and drilling and cleaving direction per specification and authority and review the securing plan, and any plan change must leave a trail; when a securing or direction uncertainty or a hidden material risk is found, stop first and review, and do not continue processing without authorization
Scenario | A gemstone awaiting processing shows signs of internal tension under magnification, and the site is advised to continue cutting per the original plan to avoid delaying the delivery date.
The individual and the reviewer; the institution and quality traceability

Misjudging grading and clarity and color and cut, or missing internal characteristics and rare specimens, or errors in measurement and weight conversion; distorted grade and value determination, affecting delivery and settlement and customer relations

Determine and measure item by item per the grading system and specification and record the basis and errors, re-inspect and ask the reviewer to confirm when in doubt; when a determination or reading is in doubt, retest and review immediately, and do not modify conclusions without authorization or force a certificate through

Scenario | The clarity or color determination of the same gemstone differs from the reviewer's conclusion, and the site is advised to fill in the record at the higher grade first so as not to affect the sale.
The individual and the reviewer; the institution and customers and regulatory inspection

Clarity diagrams and measurement and valuation and maintenance records that are untrue, missing or modified after the fact without a trail; distorted quality traceability and value determination, and dispute handling and inspection lacking a basis

Record grading, measurement, valuation bases and handling truthfully per procedure; when errors or omissions are found, keep the original record and note the correction time, basis and reviewer, and do not backdate, alter or fill in untested data by guesswork.

Scenario | At shift handover the previous batch's grading diagrams and measurement readings are found to be missing or inconsistent, and the staff are advised to fill in according to the report basis to avoid being questioned about the difference.
The individual and the process supervisor; the institution and customers

Issuing grading or value conclusions beyond authority, or replacing third-party testing and settlement with a determination; conclusions beyond authority and capability may mislead customers and cause legal and reputational consequences

Grading and value conclusions are issued per institutional procedure and authority, and matters involving certificates and final determination and disputes are handed to a senior grader or testing institution; when a request exceeds the authorized scope, first explain the boundary and hand it over per process
Scenario | A customer asks for an immediate value conclusion and promises it can be used for transaction settlement, while institutional procedure requires a senior grader to review it first.
The individual and the crew; the institution and delivery continuity

A key process is borne by a single person, and grading and processing and certificate issuance are interrupted during leave or equipment failure; delivery delays and customer dissatisfaction and disruption to institutional operations

Establish handover and backup arrangements for key processes, with parameters and bases and pending items clearly on the record, and hand over equipment and tool status; when staffing or equipment is insufficient, report per procedure and adjust priorities, and do not rush work with hidden risks
Scenario | The only colleague familiar with a certain grading or processing process is on leave, and the crew is asked to have untrained personnel fill in temporarily to maintain capacity.
The individual and sales or business positions; the institution and customers

Unclear delivery and acceptance standards, and customer expectations of grade or dimensions or appearance inconsistent with the conclusions; returns and rework and claim disputes and reputational loss

Before delivery, confirm the grade and dimensions and appearance and acceptance basis with the customer or business position and leave a trail, keeping the measurement and diagram and photo basis; when expectations are inconsistent, pause delivery and review the basis, and do not verbally promise anything beyond the conclusion
Scenario | A customer raises an objection about grade or dimensions when picking up goods at the store, and the site is asked to deliver first and verbally promise later adjustment.

entries.answer: This page's Gem and Diamond Workers corresponds to US SOC 51-9071.06: fabricate, finish, or evaluate the quality of gems and diamonds used in jewelry or industrial tools. The core work includes assigning polish and symmetry and clarity grades to stones according to an established grading system; recording clarity characteristics with diagrams; examining the surface and internal structure with optical instruments such as polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes to distinguish species and identify rare specimens or find flaws; locating and marking drilling or cutting positions on stones; securing stones with fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks; selecting grinding wheels and mixing and applying abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents; polishing facets and holding stones against rotating laps and wheels and saws for cutting and shaping and grinding; measuring drilling and facet dimensions with precision measuring instruments; grading rough diamonds by shape and size and color and quality; cleaving stones along pre-marked lines to remove flaws; determining specific gravity and key properties with prescribed chemical solutions; estimating wholesale and retail value from price guides and market fluctuations; replacing and truing and sharpening blades and drills and laps and maintaining equipment; and advising customers on stone selection and buying and selling diamonds and diamond jewelry. Common employers include jewelry manufacturing and retail enterprises, gem and diamond grading and trading organizations, testing and appraisal institutions and industrial diamond and abrasive product companies; what is described here is the US occupational classification basis.
entries.question: What exactly does this occupation do?

entries.answer: The core difference lies in the object and the output: this occupation takes unworked gems and diamonds as its object, and its output is verifiable grading and clarity diagrams and measurement readings and processed facets and dimensions and the valuation basis; jewelers and precious stone and metal workers (51-9071 series, jewelry making direction) take precious metals and jewelry structures and settings as their object; hand grinders and polishers (51-9023.00) produce the hand grinding and polishing of general workpieces; grinding machine workers (51-4033.00) produce the operation of grinding and lapping and polishing equipment for metal and plastic workpieces; etchers and engravers (51-9194.00) produce etching and engraving on surfaces such as metal and glass; dental laboratory technicians (51-9081.00) produce dental restorations. The objects and outputs all differ, and grade determination and value determination and processing parameters cannot be carried over across positions.

This description does not replace employer requirements for safety and equipment and process training and quality system confirmation; the actual requirements are subject to institutional and position requirements.
entries.question: What education and training are needed?

entries.answer: Having been trained, completing a course or obtaining a certificate, completing an apprenticeship, passing institutional assessment, and obtaining institutional authority are different states. The O*NET certificate catalog lists related certificates awarded by industry bodies (such as the American Gem Society's Certified Gemologist, Certified Sales Associate and Certified Gemologist Appraiser), but a certificate catalog is not the same as institutional grading issuance authority or value determination authority or regulatory permission; work involving rotating equipment and chemicals and soldering must be trained and authorized per institutional safety procedures and competent authority requirements. In mainland China, grading and appraisal of jewelry, jade and gemstone items has formed industry and group standards with vocational training and skill level evaluation, and an individual's course or certificate does not automatically equal institutional grading issuance or value determination or transaction settlement authority.
entries.question: Are certificates or qualifications needed?

entries.answer: Common failures include: misjudging the cutting or drilling or cleaving direction or improper securing causing chipping or fracture and irreversible material loss; errors in polish and symmetry and clarity and color and cut determination or missed internal characteristics or measurement and conversion errors; clarity diagrams and measurement and valuation and maintenance records that are untrue, missing or modified after the fact without a trail; issuing grading or value conclusions beyond authority or replacing third-party testing and settlement with a determination; a key process borne by a single person causing delivery interruption; unclear delivery and acceptance standards causing returns and claims; and leakage of customer identity and transaction and inventory and price information. The control points are checking and reviewing and leaving a trail per institutional standards and specification and authority, stopping and escalating anomalies and out-of-authority matters, and prioritizing material safety and customer asset protection. Error correction must keep the original record and note the correction time, basis and reviewer, and must not backdate or fill in numbers by guesswork.

subject.name: Gem and Diamond Workers
subject.summary: Gem and Diamond Workers corresponds to US O*NET/SOC 51-9071.06 Gem and Diamond Workers: fabricate, finish, or evaluate the quality of gems and diamonds used in jewelry or industrial tools. Assign polish, symmetry and clarity grades to stones according to an established grading system; record clarity characteristics with diagrams; examine the surface and internal structure of stones with optical instruments such as polariscopes and refractometers and microscopes to distinguish species, identify rare specimens or find flaws; locate and mark drilling or cutting positions on stones; secure stones with fixtures and chucks and dop sticks and blocks; select grinding wheels and mix and apply abrasives and diamond bort and polishing agents; polish facets and hold stones against rotating laps and wheels and saws for cutting and shaping and grinding; measure drilling and facet dimensions with precision measuring instruments; grade rough diamonds by shape and size and color and quality; cleave stones along pre-marked lines to remove flaws; determine specific gravity and key properties with prescribed chemical solutions; estimate wholesale and retail value from price guides and market fluctuations; replace, true and sharpen blades and drills and laps and maintain equipment; and advise customers on stone selection and buy and sell diamonds and diamond jewelry. Official scope text: Fabricate, finish, or evaluate the quality of gems and diamonds used in jewelry or industrial tools.
